text: Mastitis (udder inflammation, caused by bacteria entering through injury or the teat canal) can significantly cut milk production. Most cases affect only one quarter, with the other three producing normally. Acute cases: the affected quarter is swollen, hot, red, and produces little milk; fever, depression, and shivering are common, and the cow may flinch or kick when the udder is touched due to sensitivity. Sub-acute/chronic cases: no fever or general illness, but low milk output and a tough/firm quarter — the cow resists the calf trying to nurse, leaving the calf hungry and losing condition. Treatment (best started early): inject 5 ml Oxytocin to help drain the udder; hand-milk out the affected quarter twice a day for 2 days (restrain the cow in a crush, since this is painful for her); inject antibiotics (Sulfa+TMP or Amoxicillin) for 3 days; if the udder is very hard, a single Dexamethasone or Tolfedine injection helps reduce inflammation.
